<h1>Predicting Weight from Waist Girth and Height: Does the Relationship Differ by Gender?</h1>
<p><em>Pranav Abhinand Iyer — July 28, 2026</em></p>

<h2>Introduction</h2>
<p>Our dataset contains 21 skeletal and girth body measurements, along with age, weight, height, and gender,
for 507 adults (260 women, 247 men). Measurements were collected by Heinz, Peterson, and colleagues at
San José State University, the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School, and California health clubs, mostly on
individuals in their twenties and thirties who exercised regularly. All measurements are complete; the
codebook reports no missing values, so no observations were dropped from our analysis.</p>

<h3>Code book</h3>
<table>
<tr><th>Variable</th><th>Description</th><th>Units</th><th>Role</th></tr>
<tr><td><code>weight_kg</code></td><td>Body weight</td><td>kilograms</td><td>Outcome</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>waist_girth</code></td><td>Waist girth, narrowest part of the torso below the rib cage</td><td>centimeters</td><td>Predictor of primary interest</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>height_cm</code></td><td>Standing height</td><td>centimeters</td><td>Predictor (control)</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>gender</code></td><td>Self-reported sex, recoded from source 0/1 code</td><td>Female / Male</td><td>Predictor / interaction</td></tr>
</table>
<p><strong>Omitted variables:</strong> the remaining 21 skeletal/girth measurements and age are omitted — see
full justification in <code>Analysis.qmd</code>.</p>

<h3>Motivation and question</h3>
<p>Waist girth is a simple, low-cost proxy for body composition, but men and women differ systematically in
fat distribution patterns. <strong>Question:</strong> Can we predict an adult's weight from waist girth and
height, and does that relationship differ between men and women?</p>
<ul>
<li><em>Primary:</em> H0: β<sub>waist</sub> = 0 vs. Ha: β<sub>waist</sub> &gt; 0</li>
<li><em>Interaction:</em> H0: β<sub>waist×male</sub> = 0 vs. Ha: β<sub>waist×male</sub> ≠ 0</li>
</ul>

<h2>Methods</h2>
<p>Multiple linear regression: weight ~ waist girth × gender + height, with waist girth and height
mean-centered to remove structural collinearity with the interaction term. Modeling used base R
<code>lm()</code>, tidied with <code>broom</code>, checked with <code>car::vif()</code>, plotted with
<code>ggplot2</code>.</p>

<table>
<tr><th>Gender</th><th>n</th><th>Mean weight (kg)</th><th>SD weight (kg)</th><th>Mean waist girth (cm)</th><th>Mean height (cm)</th></tr>
<tr><td>Female</td><td>260</td><td>62.1</td><td>10.0</td><td>71.4</td><td>164.9</td></tr>
<tr><td>Male</td><td>247</td><td>76.6</td><td>11.4</td><td>82.9</td><td>177.9</td></tr>
</table>

<h2>Results</h2>
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Main scatterplot">
<p><em>Figure 1 (primary result). Weight vs. waist girth by gender, with fitted regression lines.</em></p>

<table>
<tr><th>Term</th><th>Estimate</th><th>Std. Error</th><th>p-value</th></tr>
<tr><td>Intercept</td><td>71.212</td><td>0.407</td><td>&lt; .001</td></tr>
<tr><td>Waist girth (cm, centered)</td><td>1.025</td><td>0.036</td><td>&lt; .001</td></tr>
<tr><td>Gender: Male (vs. Female)</td><td>-3.112</td><td>0.612</td><td>&lt; .001</td></tr>
<tr><td>Height (cm, centered)</td><td>0.519</td><td>0.029</td><td>&lt; .001</td></tr>
<tr><td>Waist girth x Male</td><td>-0.149</td><td>0.048</td><td>= 0.002</td></tr>
</table>

<p>R² = 0.892, adjusted R² = 0.892, n = 507. Each additional cm of waist girth predicts +1.03 kg of weight
among women (p &lt; .001, holding height constant); the interaction term (p = 0.002) shows this slope is
about 0.15 kg/cm <em>smaller</em> for men (≈0.88 kg/cm) — supporting the interaction hypothesis.</p>

<h3>Model diagnostics</h3>
<div class="figrow">
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Residuals vs fitted">
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="QQ plot">
</div>
<p>No strong pattern in residuals vs. fitted (supports linearity/constant variance); Q-Q plot shows
approximate normality with modest tail deviation (Shapiro-Wilk p &lt; .001, but n = 507 makes this a minor
concern). All VIFs &lt; 5 after centering (multicollinearity not a substantial issue).</p>

<h2>Discussion</h2>
<p>Waist girth strongly predicts weight, and — as hypothesized — the relationship is stronger for women than
men, even controlling for height. The slope difference (~0.15 kg/cm) is modest but statistically clear given
the sample size and measurement precision, consistent with known sex differences in fat distribution.</p>
<p><strong>Limitations:</strong> convenience sample of young, active Californians (not generalizable);
observational/cross-sectional (association, not causation); modest residual non-normality. A residual
gender gap in weight persisted even at matched waist girth and height — worth exploring with additional
predictors like body frame or age.</p>
